title: Light as a circadian stimulus for architectural lighting

findings.quote: Empirically, nocturnal melatonin suppression in humans was shown in two independent studies6,7 to have a peak spectral sensitivity at 460 nm and a 110-nm wide absorption band at half-maximum sensitivity.

findings.antecedent: Melanopsin photopigment (after pre-retinal filtering by human crystalline lens)
findings.quote: Direct measurements of the action spectrum for melanopsin in human ipRGCs show a peak spectral sensitivity at approximately 479 nm22... with pre-retinal filtering... peak sensitivity shifts to approximately 484 nm and the half-maximum sensitivity bandwidth is about 90 nm

findings.antecedent: Light characterized by log10 Circadian Light (CLA) (equation 1)
findings.quote: Among these three possible characterizations of light for the human circadian system, CLA best characterizes the spectral sensitivity of nocturnal melatonin suppression data. ... with CLA (r2=0.91)

findings.antecedent: Light characterized by log10 melanopsin-weighted irradiance
findings.quote: ...melanopsin-weighted irradiance (r2=0.87), it is important to note that the regression errors in Figure 4(b) are systematically larger than those in Figure 4(c) for the short-wavelength data...

findings.antecedent: Light characterized by log10 photopic illuminance
findings.quote: Figure 4 shows the nocturnal melatonin suppression values... as a function of log10 photopic illuminance (Figure 4(a))... (r2 = 0.38)

findings.antecedent: Circadian Stimulus (CS) from polychromatic light sources
findings.quote: Figure 5 serves to illustrate the validity of the circadian phototransduction model (equations (1) and (2)) for predicting nocturnal melatonin suppression from polychromatic sources

findings.antecedent: CS value of 0.3 or higher (from waking to 6:00 pm)
findings.consequent: Sleep quality, sleep duration, symptoms of depression and agitation in Alzheimer's patients
findings.quote: Figueiro et al.15,36,40 showed that exposing Alzheimer's disease patients to a CS of 0.3 or higher from waking to 6:00 pm improved sleep quality, increased sleep duration, and reduced symptoms of depression and agitation.

findings.antecedent: Average CS values (summer months ~0.3 vs. winter months <0.2) in office workers
findings.quote: Figueiro and Rea37 showed that office workers in summer months had greater sleep duration and efficiency than in winter months. ... average CS values were close to 0.3 while the average CS exposure in winter months was less than 0.2.

findings.antecedent: CS greater than 0.3 in the morning hours (8:00 am to noon) for office workers
findings.consequent: Sleep onset, sleep quality, disturbed sleep, depression
findings.quote: Unpublished data... show that... office workers who receive a CS greater than 0.3 in the morning hours fell asleep earlier, reported having better sleep quality, less disturbed sleep, and feeling less depressed.

findings.antecedent: Lighting installation delivering a CS of at least 0.3 in submariners
findings.consequent: Measures of circadian entrainment (total melatonin in first morning urine void), sleep efficiency, self-reports of sleepiness
findings.quote: Young et al.35 showed that exposing submariners to a lighting installation delivering a CS of at least 0.3, increased measures of circadian entrainment... increased sleep efficiency, as measured by actigraphy and reduced self-reports of sleepiness during the shift.

findings.consequent: Functional impact of 'cool' light sources (high proportion of short-wavelength radiation)
findings.quote: Thus, the functional impact of light sources with a high proportion of short-wavelength radiation (i.e., 'cool' sources) will be systematically underestimated using a metric based upon melanopsin-weighted irradiance.

findings.antecedent: 40 lux to 200 lux at the eye of a 640-nm (red) light
findings.quote: 40 lux to 200 lux at the eye of a 640-nm (red) light has been shown to enhance brain activity during the day and night without affecting melatonin concentrations.45,46

limitations: Knowledge about the human circadian system is incomplete.
Neural signals from the retina can reach the SCN without conduction through ipRGC axons, but these connections are limited.
The Circadian Stimulus (CS) metric is incomplete.
Other lighting characteristics that affect the circadian system (timing, duration, distribution, and photic history) are not considered in the CS metric.
No consideration is given to the spectral and absolute sensitivity of the non-visual alerting effects of light exposure in the CS metric.
The spectral reflectances of architectural materials must be considered in CS calculations.
The ideas expressed are based on the authors' experience and insights and have not been vetted among the entire community of lighting stakeholders.
minimum_safe_summary: This theoretical paper proposes and validates the Circadian Stimulus (CS) metric for quantifying light's impact on the human circadian system in architectural spaces. It argues that the CS metric, derived from a biophysical model of retinal phototransduction, better characterizes nocturnal melatonin suppression (R²=0.91) than melanopsin-weighted irradiance (R²=0.87) or photopic illuminance (R²=0.38). The paper presents evidence from laboratory and field studies showing the CS metric's predictive validity for outcomes like melatonin suppression, sleep quality, sleep duration, circadian entrainment, and reduced depression and agitation. Limitations include the incompleteness of current knowledge about the circadian system, the CS metric's current exclusion of factors like light timing, duration, distribution, photic history, and non-visual alerting effects, and the need for broader stakeholder vetting.
